newsitem.title: USA: Incumbent leads vote in Pittsburgh mayoral primary.
newsitem.headline: Incumbent leads vote in Pittsburgh mayoral primary.

text.p: Mayor Tom Murphy led Tuesday's Democratic primary by a comfortable margin after fending off an early challenge by city Councilman Bob O'Connor.

With 91 percent of precincts reporting, Murphy had 53 percent of the vote, compared with O'Connor's 42 percent. A third challenger, community activist Chaston Roston, held on to 5 percent of the vote.
Harry Frost is the sole Republican candidate.
Early returns showed O'Connor with a small lead, but Murphy quickly pulled ahead and continued to widen his lead as more precincts reported.
Murphy, who built his campaign on his record of redeveloping struggling city neighbourhoods, has pledged not to raise taxes in his second term.

"We're going to take Pittsburgh forward," Murphy told supporters at his campaign headquarters. "We've had the toughest 20 years in the city's history. We lost a whole industry (steel.) We can't stay there. We're going to take Pittsburgh forward."
Pittsburgh, a heavily Democratic city, has not elected a Republican mayor since 1931.

Meanwhile, a controversial referendum on whether to create a seven-member civilian review board to monitor citizen complaints against police appeared to be on the verge of passing. With 91 percent of precincts reporting, 58 percent of voters supported the measure, and 42 percent were opposed.

Discussions about creating a civilian review board have taken place in Pittsburgh for several years but gained momentum after October 1995, when Jonny Gammage, a black motorist, died while in the custody of five white police officers.
Police officials said creating a board might prevent some officers from using what they see as necessary force.
"I think (officers) will be a lot more hesitant," Steve Crisanti, a city police officer, said. "We won't be as aggressive."
